video_title: Brij Khurana, Fixed Income Portfolio Manager, Wellington
gist: Wellington unconstrained bond PM Brij Khurana argues low rates financialized the economy, that inflation is now wealth-driven, and that priced Fed and global hikes look excessive versus nominal growth. He favors inflation-linked bonds, global bonds in rate-sensitive economies and EM local bonds.

insights.claim: Non-residential investment has been its own cycle since the 2000-2001 internet bubble crash and is not highly correlated with interest rates, undermining the neo-Keynesian models the Fed relies on; today AI capex shows almost no correlation to rates that Khurana considers really high.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Rate cuts may not stimulate real investment, so the Fed's policy transmission is weaker than models assume.
insights.quote: there is almost no correlation to the AI capex investment that we're seeing

insights.claim: Negative real rates encouraged financialization: household releveraging in the early 2000s, corporate buybacks and private equity consolidation after the GFC, then government borrowing after COVID that funded consumption rather than investment; Khurana argues this reduced competition, lowered the structural real rate and cut potential growth.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Prolonged zero-rate policy may have left a lower-growth, more asset-dependent economy.

insights.claim: Because the US is capital-markets dominated, deeply negative policy rates would have led US companies to borrow and buy back stock, whereas in bank-centric Europe negative rates squeezed bank profits and lending.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Negative-rate experience in Europe should not be extrapolated to the US.

insights.claim: Khurana argues QE did not lower yields via the balance-sheet channel; larger Fed balance sheets raised yields because markets fear debt monetization and buy reflationary assets like stocks instead of bonds, so stocks rose because discount rates rose, not fell.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet shrinkage under a new Fed chair could be bond-friendly rather than bearish, contrary to the consensus mechanism.

insights.claim: Core CPI excluding shelter has run around 2% for roughly three years, and Khurana contends the labor market is in balance and wages are not the source of inflation; residual sticky services inflation (shelter, medical care, restaurants, travel) is tied to the wealth effect and past fiscal spending.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Raising the policy rate targets labor-demand inflation that is no longer the problem, so hikes may be an ill-fitted tool.

insights.claim: Baby boomers control roughly 50-60% of US wealth with an asset allocation of about 70-75% stocks, and US household wealth in stocks now exceeds real estate for the first time, so wealth concentrated in equities drives demand and services inflation.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: An equity drawdown would hit consumption and services inflation more than usual; policy that targets wages would be more effective than rate hikes.

insights.claim: Wages as a percent of GDP have fallen over time and asset prices have outgrown nominal growth; Khurana says the most desirable outcome would be real wage growth to grow into the current asset price levels, echoing Secretary Bessent's real economy versus Wall Street framing.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Inflation stays sticky as long as distribution is skewed toward asset owners.

themes.theme: Fed hikes, growth risk and the US curve

insights.claim: Markets price close to 100bp of Fed hikes, bringing the policy rate near 5% after one hike, with Europe pricing about 80bp and Australia and New Zealand also pricing hikes, a coordinated global tightening that follows a year and a half of global loosening.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Support from global easing that fueled strong growth is reversing at once.

insights.claim: Khurana notes the two classic recession causes, tight monetary policy and commodity price shocks, are both emerging: real wages ex-transfers are growing negatively year over year because of the oil shock, and consumer balance sheets are weaker than in 2022-23 when the Fed funds peak was similar.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Nominal growth likely peaked over the last year, and pricing for continued hikes looks vulnerable.

insights.claim: A fiscal impulse front-loaded by the One Big Beautiful Bill in the first half of the year may fade, and divided government after the November election has historically been an important inflection for bond markets as the market prices less stimulus.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: November is a potential bond-market catalyst.

insights.claim: The 2s10s curve has not inverted spot but is inverted in forward space a year out, meaning the market implies that if the Fed follows through with hikes, policy will become tight enough to invert the curve.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Forward inversion signals the market doubts the full hiking path will be sustainable.

insights.claim: Khurana attributes the recent rise in yields mainly to a Fed repricing and an AI-driven real growth story, not Treasury supply or inflation expectations, which are low and anchored to 2% on Fed credibility.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Supply fears are overstated as the driver of the selloff; the back end follows the front end.

insights.claim: Khurana estimates fair 10-year-10-year forward yield near 5 to 5.25%: about 1.5% long-term real growth (0.5% population, 1% productivity), 2.5% inflation giving 4% nominal growth, plus roughly 100bp of term premium for higher debt; the 10y10y forward near 6.2% is about 100bp too high.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Long-dated Treasuries look cheap against his nominal-growth anchor, supporting a duration-long view if growth slows.

insights.claim: The back end would rally only if markets signal the hikes are a mistake, as in the 2018 episode when the Christmas selloff in stocks of over 20% forced a Fed U-turn; stocks currently show no such signal, though Khurana expects the question to arise after the election.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Equities, not bonds, need to break first for the Fed to pivot.

insights.claim: Because US consumption is relatively insensitive to rates, thanks to widespread fixed-rate mortgages locked in during 2020-21, the Fed must move rates much more to have an economic impact, making the front end of the US curve more volatile than other markets.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Expect larger front-end volatility in the US than in variable-rate markets.

themes.theme: AI capex, credit and bank regulation

insights.claim: Some AI chip financing deals look circular, recalling pre-GFC lending; bank loans to non-depository financial institutions have grown by close to a trillion dollars over six or seven years, meaning banks are effectively lending to private credit under favorable capital treatment.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Risk is migrating back to banks indirectly, contradicting the view that private credit insulates the banking system.

insights.claim: Khurana predicts the Fed will probably lower capital ratios on loans to non-depository financial institutions given historically low defaults and low LTVs, though he argues it should raise them to bring the lending under regulatory oversight.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Regulatory loosening could feed further credit growth into AI and private credit.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers issue at record IG levels and do not mind paying 6-8% because they assume 30-40% returns on AI investment, which crowds out other corporate borrowers and pressures spreads for them.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Insensitivity to rates makes AI borrowing pro-cyclical for yields and supply-heavy for the long end.

insights.claim: AI borrowing is so large that nominal growth cannot slow easily, so bonds fail as a growth hedge, stock-bond correlation rises, and demand for bonds falls, pushing yields higher, a second form of crowding out.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Portfolio diversification from duration is weaker; higher term premium is justified.

themes.theme: Global rates and EM local opportunity

insights.claim: Khurana sees mistaken hiking cycles priced in Australia, New Zealand and the UK, comparing them to the ECB's 2008 hike: unemployment is rising, inflation is oil-driven supply-side, and variable-rate mortgages give quick pass-through, so these markets could rally.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Long positions in these bond markets, hedged to dollars, can yield more than Treasuries.

insights.claim: Emerging market local bonds returned almost 18% last year and are still positive this year while fixed income is flat to negative; real policy rates of 4-8%, cheap real exchange rates, low fiscal spending and market-friendly politics in Argentina, Colombia, Hungary and Chile suggest early innings of a bull market with light investor allocation.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: EM local bonds are a structural overweight in an unconstrained bond portfolio.

insights.claim: Chinese five-year yields near 1.5% are below even safe-haven markets like Switzerland, which Khurana reads as the bond market pricing a balance-sheet recession after the housing bust, similar to the US and Europe after the GFC; he sees little to do there.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Chinese rates are a deleveraging signal, not an opportunity.

insights.claim: The August 2024 yen carry unwind correlated with US stocks more than EM or bonds, because yen carry money now goes into US equities rather than EM assets or Treasuries; Japan matters more for equities than for bonds.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Yen moves are an equity risk factor first.

insights.claim: Khurana reads Bessent's Japan focus as an attempt to stabilize the yen so that hedging US assets stops being a one-way trade, repatriating capital to Japanese bonds; this implies Japanese buying of Treasuries declines, a contradiction since someone else must buy them.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: US policy may shift marginal Treasury buyer demands to other holders.

insights.claim: The UK gilt market is cleaner than during the 2022 Truss episode: long issuance has been cut, QT outright sales are being scaled back, and even left-leaning governments are responsive to the bond market, though 85-100bp of BoE hikes are priced; Khurana sees more optimism on UK gilts than in recent years.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: UK back end looks relatively attractive versus the US, which keeps spending regardless of yields.

insights.claim: The French-German spread is wider than in 2011 because France went through a 15-year credit boom while Italy and Greece deleveraged, but Khurana says pricing France like 2011 Italy is unreasonable since euro exit is not possible and the ECB has more tools to buy French debt.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Tail-risk scenarios for French spreads are being overpriced.

insights.claim: Khurana ranks inflation-linked bonds near the top of his list: breakevens are around 2.3% across the curve with little inflation risk premium while real yields are the highest since the 1990s launch, though nominals would outperform in a growth slowdown.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Cheap inflation insurance with attractive real carry versus credit.

insights.claim: TIPS breakevens stay low because linkers trade like a risk asset and are less liquid than Treasuries, and because they disappointed investors in 2022 by posting negative total returns despite beating nominals, leaving the asset class underowned.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: The low-breakeven anomaly stems from technical ownership issues, not fundamentals.

insights.claim: Khurana notes that 5-year real yields rose about 100-130bp over six months, one of the largest increases on record, yet the 5-year TIPS real yield was 3.5% when first issued in the 1990s, so real yields could go higher.
insights.speaker: Brij Khurana
insights.so_what: Yields are high versus recent history but not extreme historically.
